final_feedback: I accuse Justin Tyme. He had historical source familiarity, preview exposure, an admitted visit to the unattended glass, a personal conflict over Grant discrediting his property story, and the uniquely false claim that the later clipping established neutralization. That claim conflicts with the actual clipping and laboratory evidence and protects the murder mechanism rather than an incidental embarrassment. Strongest alternative Anya Tique explicitly used a working cupboard key after preview and could obtain poison; Chip also knows the seal. Neither has comparably established drink opportunity or a lie denying the active source. Confidence is high within the game’s witness-contradiction convention, but this is not a complete physical proof: there is no observation of Justin obtaining poison or uniquely matched seal fragment. The voices contain distinct concerns but share rhythmic, literate confession-and-address structures. All thirty have a Grant conflict, an object or document adjustment, then a personal admission; this repeated arrangement is conspicuous. Payroll, caregiving, professional shame and family belonging are plausible stakes, though many financial disputes resolve with remarkably prompt refunds or corrections. Staff-accessible poison storage and an unattended donor glass are feasible after the stated staging, but allowing an unresolved historic cyanide bottle on an open bench despite explicit warnings is hard to credit. Deduction works through linked custody, material and document comparisons, yet final culprit identification rests disproportionately on the one late false defense. Emotional consequences are strongest in stage eight; dialogue rarely changes another speaker’s response in real time. Unresolved conflict survives in canceled workshops, unauthorized payroll, source protection, family calls and shame, but most side arcs close too neatly.
protocol_deviation: None. Checkpoints read sequentially and scores saved before opening the next.
post_vote_feedback: The reveal confirms Justin and supplies his exact source-taking action at the preview and glass poisoning. The essential contradiction was already available before voting: the clipping lacked neutralization and the source retained active cyanide. His confession therefore confirms the solution rather than introducing its central disproof. However, his presence at the preview and acquisition of poison were not explicitly established in his earlier account; my pre-vote wording that he saw the source at preview overstated an inference from historical familiarity and the general open-preview opportunity. The confession adds that missing physical link. A pre-vote observation placing him beside the bottle would strengthen a genuinely player-led proof. The endings are unusually humane about ongoing harm: Tess retains an unanswered argument, Brie has crying staff and unpaid cheese, Cary fears his job, Anne owes displaced guests an explanation, and restitution remains unresolved. Sue/Mona and Vincent/Dada have relationships that can continue beyond cleared suspicion. Yet every ending recites exculpatory evidence, confesses an adjacent fault, then pivots to a personal lesson or another named guest. The recurring therapeutic self-awareness and orderly reconciliation flatten voices; several endings sound written to satisfy an editorial template. Justin’s remembered-history versus invented-history reversal is apt but too eloquently resolved for a fresh confession. No scores or pre-vote accusation were changed after reveal.
